blocks.prompt: The Animal Doctor
blocks.text: A vet is a doctor for animals. Animals cannot say where it hurts. So the vet has to be a good detective. The vet watches how an animal moves. She feels its tummy with her hands. She listens to its heart with a stethoscope. She looks in its ears and mouth. A vet gives shots that keep animals from getting sick. She fixes broken bones and sore teeth. Some vets take care of cats and dogs. Other vets drive to farms to help big cows and horses. Every vet wants animals to feel well.

blocks.prompt: The Doctor Who Cannot Ask What Hurts
blocks.text: When you feel sick, you can tell a doctor exactly what is wrong. You can say your throat hurts or your tummy aches. Animals cannot do this. That is why being a vet is such interesting work. A vet has to read clues instead of words. A limping dog, a cat that will not eat, a horse that keeps shaking its head: each of these is a message the vet must figure out. To read those clues, a vet learns the bodies of many different animals. A human doctor studies just one kind of body, the human one. A vet may treat a hamster in the morning and a horse in the afternoon, and those two animals are built in very different ways. A vet knows how fast a rabbit's heart should beat and how a snake breathes. Vets do far more than treat sick animals. They give shots that stop diseases before they start. They clean teeth, set broken bones, and help animals have babies safely. Some vets care for pets, some care for farm animals, and some care for lions and seals at the zoo.

blocks.prompt: A Doctor for Every Animal
blocks.text: A human doctor spends a whole career learning one species: people. A veterinarian takes on a harder problem. The animal kingdom is enormous, and a vet may be asked to treat almost any part of it. A dog and a parrot and a goat do not share the same heartbeat, the same diet, or the same way of showing pain, yet a vet is expected to help them all. Because animals cannot describe their symptoms, a vet has to diagnose without a single spoken word. Diagnosing means working out what is wrong from evidence alone. The vet observes how the animal stands and moves, feels for swelling, listens to the lungs, checks the temperature, and sometimes takes an x-ray or a blood test. A twitching ear or a dull coat can be an important clue. Much of a vet's work is not treatment but prevention. Vaccinating an animal means giving it a small, safe dose that trains its body to fight a disease later. A vet who vaccinates a herd of cattle may stop an outbreak before it begins. Vets also guard human health. Many dangerous diseases, including rabies, can pass from animals to people, so a vet who keeps animals healthy is protecting families too. Vets work in many places. Some run clinics for pets. Some drive from farm to farm caring for livestock. Others work in zoos, aquariums, wildlife parks, or laboratories. Wherever animals are, a vet is usually not far away.

blocks.prompt: The Hardest Kind of Doctor
blocks.text: Ask most people to picture a veterinarian, and they imagine someone cuddling a puppy. The reality is far more demanding. A physician trains for years to understand one species. A veterinarian is asked to understand hundreds, from a two-gram finch to a two-ton bull, and to switch between them in a single working day. That breadth creates a genuine problem: the patient can never explain what is wrong. A person can point to an aching knee. An animal can only limp, or hide, or stop eating. Some animals, especially prey species like rabbits and birds, actively conceal illness, because in the wild a creature that looks weak is the one a predator chooses. So the vet becomes an investigator, gathering evidence the patient is trying to hide. Posture, breathing, temperature, the feel of an abdomen, the results of blood work and imaging: each is a clue in a case with no confession. Veterinary medicine is also older and broader than many people assume. The first veterinary school opened in Lyon, France, in 1761, founded by a horseman named Claude Bourgelat, at a time when working animals powered farms, armies, and cities. The very word veterinary comes from a Latin term for beasts of burden. For centuries the job was mostly about keeping horses and cattle useful. Only recently has the family pet moved to the center of the profession. Perhaps the most overlooked part of a vet's work is protecting people. A large share of human diseases, including rabies, bird flu, and many kinds of food poisoning, begin in animals. When a vet inspects a herd, vaccinates a dog, or spots a sick bird early, the barrier they build protects human families as much as animal ones. Doctors and veterinarians, it turns out, are guarding the same border from opposite sides. A vet, then, is not simply an animal lover in a white coat. A vet is a detective who works without a witness, a specialist in dozens of bodies at once, and a quiet guardian of human health. It is one of the hardest kinds of doctoring there is.

6.title: The Doctor Who Cannot Ask What Hurts
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Doctor Who Cannot Ask What Hurts

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Veterinary is Latin for beasts of burden
First vet school opened in Lyon in 1761
Zoonoses: diseases shared by animals and people
One Health links animal, human, and environment
Prey species conceal weakness to avoid predators
Vets know normal vital signs for dozens of species

blocks.prompt: The Detective Who Works Without a Witness
blocks.text: A physician and a veterinarian both begin with the same goal, a healthy patient, but the veterinarian starts from a much harder position. A doctor of humans studies a single species across an entire career. A veterinarian is expected to hold in mind the anatomy, diet, temperament, and normal vital signs of dozens of species at once, and to move among them without warning. In one morning a small-animal vet might examine a cat, a rabbit, a lizard, and a cockatoo, four creatures whose bodies agree on almost nothing. This breadth is the first thing that makes veterinary medicine so difficult, and it is invisible to most of the people who drop off a sick puppy and expect a quick answer. The second difficulty is deeper: the patient cannot speak, and often does not want to be understood. A human describes the ache and points to the spot. An animal offers only behavior, and prey animals go further and lie. A rabbit or a bird will hide the very symptoms a vet needs to see, because in the wild, visible weakness is an invitation to a predator. The vet, therefore, is a detective working a case in which the victim actively destroys the evidence. Diagnosis becomes a craft of inference: reading posture, coat, breathing rate, the temperature of an ear, the tension in an abdomen, the shadows on an x-ray, and assembling those fragments into an explanation the animal will never confirm. It is worth remembering how old and how practical this profession is. The first veterinary school opened in Lyon, France, in 1761, founded by Claude Bourgelat during an age when horses and oxen were the engines of farms and armies. The word veterinary itself descends from a Latin term meaning beasts of burden. For most of its history, the field existed to keep working animals working. The house cat and the family dog are recent arrivals at the center of the vet's attention. The least visible part of the work may be the most important. Roughly six in ten known human infectious diseases can pass between animals and people, a category scientists call zoonoses, and rabies, bird flu, and many forms of food poisoning belong to it. Every time a veterinarian vaccinates a dog, inspects a herd of cattle, or isolates a sick bird, they are reinforcing a barrier that guards human families as directly as animal ones. This idea now has a name, One Health, the recognition that the wellbeing of animals, people, and the shared environment cannot be separated. Put these threads together and the cuddly image dissolves. A veterinarian is a specialist in many bodies rather than one, a detective who must solve cases without a cooperating witness, an inheritor of a centuries-old craft born among working horses, and a frontline guardian of human health who happens to wear the uniform of an animal lover. The white coat is real. What it conceals is a job far harder, and far more consequential, than the puppy in its arms suggests.
